The past months I attended University of California, Berkeley thanks to UC Berkeley Global Access Program and UTEC - Universidad de Ingeniería y Tecnología . The broad range of courses allowed me to pursue my passion at the intersection of Generative AI and Biology. Living in the Bay Area improved my self-efficacy by observing how other people push towards achieving their goals. I enjoyed being here, being able to learn from researchers that are on the cutting edge of their field, the friends and experiences I made along the way, and the weather in california :). I'm sure the future has compelling adventures I can participate in. And I'm always grateful for the opportunities I had. Go bears!

Today marked one of our favorite milestones of the year: Celebrating Science, our end-of-summer poster session, where RockEDU students shared the research they have spent months building alongside their mentors with our scientific community, friends, and families. Each poster was a snapshot of student research. But each poster also represented far more than a science project. It reflected weeks of curiosity, persistence, collaboration, problem-solving, and mentorship. It was a celebration of scientific discovery, and of the people and relationships that make discovery possible. This year's event brought together students from across several RockEDU pathways: ** RockEDU Undergraduate Research Scholars (RURS), which places students who complete our CURE into year-long paid research internships at Rockefeller (a program led by Jessi Hersh, PhD ) ** SSRP In Situ, led by Doug Heigl, which gives SSRP alumni the opportunity to return to Rockefeller for immersive summer research experiences in campus laboratories. ** And, of course, our longstanding Summer Science Research Program (SSRP), whose students spent the summer asking meaningful questions, learning new techniques, and contributing to research alongside outstanding scientist mentors. An event like this is the result of extraordinary care from an incredible team. Jen Bohn worked tirelessly to prepare and support our mentors, ensuring they had the tools and confidence to guide students through an authentic research experience. Jessi Hersh once again made sure every student felt supported from beginning to end, creating an environment where they could do their best work and confidently share it with others. To our RockEDU Fellows, scientist mentors, teaching teams, laboratory hosts, and support staff: thank you. The culture of learning you create is every bit as important as the science itself. We were also delighted to welcome Dannielle Kenny from Cape Town, South Africa, who spent time shadowing the SSRP as she explored ideas to bring back to her own institution. One of the greatest compliments we can receive is seeing others invest in adapting and growing these models within their own communities. We look forward to seeing where those ideas lead. Over the years, this celebration has grown into an ecosystem built through partnerships across Rockefeller and throughout New York City, where multiple entry points, sustained mentorship, and authentic research experiences help students continue to see themselves as scientists. It is exciting to see that ecosystem beginning to inspire conversations well beyond our own campus. We are incredibly proud of what our students accomplished this summer, and even more proud of the community they built together. Onward!

The View from the Office. I met up with Kaelan Yim , a rising junior studying computer science at the University of California, Berkeley, at the Bryant Park Cafe. He had quesadillas; I had the sliders. Kaelan grew up in the Bay Area. While neither of his parents worked in tech, he became interested in computer programming because of a passion for video games. He estimates he played about five hours of Minecraft a day in high school. He arrived at Berkeley planning after graduation to work on computer chip manufacturing. But friends steered his interest in the direction of AI safety research. He got a chance to work on benchmarks and evals for frontier models as a Cambridge MARS scholar and this summer he is visiting Washington for a policy program run by the Hertog Foundation with the Institute for the Study of War. One of the fun things about connecting with someone so much younger is the perspective they provide. Our conversation ranged from the percentage of Berkley students using AI to cheat on tests (high) to the red-pilled San Francisco AI culture. We covered a lot of ground, including his sense of the difference between fellowships like Z Fellows and those arranged by Thiel and the 776 Foundation as well as the evolution of Y Combinator and the recent debate over closed and open-sourced AI model builders. On the side, Kaelan does robotics research. He managed to procure a lidar sensor similar to the kind Waymo mounts on its vehicles and he’s using it to train robots recorded from a third-person perspective. He said the best thing about attending Berkeley isn’t the classes so much as the community. In education, the fundamentals still matter because you need to know the basics to understand the tech. Kaelan is a proponent of open weight models and he expects the enormous price differentials between US models from companies like Anthropic and the Chinese models like Kimi K3. He has a wide range of hobbies beyond AI including spelunking, leatherworking, glassblowing, crochet, gardening, autocross, cinema and axe throwing. He told me there are four things he wants to see during his lifespan: humans living beyond Earth, autonomous robots, fusion power, and research into human cognition. You can connect with Kaelan via LinkedIn or X or DM me for a warm intro.

This week we welcomed a new cohort of students to the 2026 Summer Science Research Program (SSRP)! Every summer, a new group of curious, thoughtful, and motivated young people walks through our doors, ready to ask questions, build skills, and experience what it means to do science. Watching that journey begin never gets old. Over the next several weeks, these students will become part of a community of researchers, mentors, educators, and peers who will learn alongside one another as they explore science through discovery. We're so excited to be on this journey with this incredible group of budding scientists. We can't wait to see where their curiosity leads. Welcome to SSRP 2026!!!

Two weeks ago, I posted about graduation, the past four years, and the honor of delivering the M.E.T. Commencement Address. Many of you asked for the video of the speech -- happy to share it here! Growing up in Silicon Valley and attending a university rooted in the heart of it all, technology and velocity are virtues drilled into our systems. Yet, when we often reminisce on college, we don’t really think back to the environments, ecosystems, or speed, but rather the stories, memories, moments, and lessons that come with them. The speech pays homage to childhood folktales from my family, memories made with my M.E.T. peers, the “hustle”-driven mentality of Cal students, the words of wisdom from my mentors, and a life lesson I’ve discovered along the way. Watch the video below, or give it a read on my website! As I wrap up the third year of my PhD, I wanted to share a couple of recent updates :)! First, I am honoured to have received an NSERC Canada Graduate Research Scholarship – Doctoral (CGRS – D). I am incredibly grateful to the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) for supporting my PhD research in supramolecular catalysis. I'm also grateful to have received an Outstanding Graduate Student Instructor (GSI) award for my time as head GSI for General Chemistry lectures at the University of California, Berkeley ! This award recognizes up to 10% of GSIs each year based on student and faculty nominations. Teaching has always been especially meaningful to me because of the positive impact that my own teachers, professors, and TAs had on my journey into chemistry. Helping students learn and succeed brings me such joy, and being recognized for that is incredibly rewarding. Thank you to my mentors, colleagues, and students for making these experiences possible. I look forward to continuing to grow as a researcher, teacher, and chemist throughout the rest of my graduate career!

I’m excited to share that I graduated University of California, Berkeley with a B.S. in Microbial Biology and a minor in Data Science. This fall, I will be continuing my education at Imperial College London , where I will pursue an MSc in Health Data Analytics and Machine Learning. I’m excited to build on my interests in biology and data science while exploring how data-driven solutions can improve health outcomes on a global scale. I am grateful to my family, friends and mentors who supported me throughout this journey. Looking forward to what comes next!🇬🇧

Four Years. Two Degrees. And a million memories to last a lifetime. This past week, I graduated from UC Berkeley's Management, Entrepreneurship, & Technology program with a dual degree in Bioengineering and Business -- still processing how fast it all went by! Berkeley (and M.E.T.) shaped my perspectives -- equipping me with the tools to think across biology, technology (especially AI), and capital markets, while introducing me to a community of deeply driven people who became close friends. I'm also grateful for everything it enabled outside the classroom: space biology research at NASA, tackling real-world diseases (like ADPKD and Dravet Syndrome) with Renasant and Regel, designing human-carrying drones with VTOL at Berkeley (shoutout Alan Zhang ), due diligence and dealflow at DraperU and Clear. Trips to Hawaii, Sonoma, and the California national parks. Late-night walks down Sather Lane. Random drives into SF. And memories with many of my peers -- including a brand-new Las Vegas Raider, Fernando Mendoza ! None of it happened alone: My family -- Mom ( Swetha Parthasarathy ), Dad ( Partha Ranganathan ), Grandfather (Thatha), and Nidhi -- has provided four years of unwavering support. And a huge thanks to my extended family/friends, who showed up at every milestone.
